name: Business Registers Interconnection System
description: BRIS is the European system that interconnects the business registers of the EU member states, reached through the “Find a company” service on the European e-Justice Portal. It gathers company information from the national registers in real time; the registers themselves remain with the member states.

publicAccess.notes: The describing pages were retrieved anonymously, but the search itself runs in an embedded application that could not be exercised, so no search behaviour is asserted and no search URL is published. The portal documents that it currently offers only information the national registers provide free of charge, and that prices shown for paid documents come from those registers and are indicative, with the final price set on the national register’s own site.

bestFor: Finding a company registered anywhere in the EU from one search, when you do not know which national register holds it.
Seeing which documents a company has filed with its national business register before going to that register to obtain them.
notRecommendedFor: Treating the result as the register entry itself. The records are constituted and held by the national business registers, not here.
Obtaining certified or paid documents. For those the portal sends you to the national register, where the final price is set.
recommendedIndustries: Companies registered in EU, Icelandic, Liechtenstein or Norwegian business registers
pros: One search reaches the business registers of every EU member state plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway, which no national register offers.
Company information is gathered from the national registers in real time rather than copied into a central store, so results reflect the source register rather than a stale snapshot.
The service is built on EU law rather than a voluntary arrangement, so participation by the national registers is an obligation rather than a courtesy.
cons: It is an interconnection layer, not a register. It does not constitute company data and it establishes nothing about a company on its own.
The search runs in an embedded application that refused automated retrieval, so its behaviour, any rate limit and any fee prompt were not observed.
Only information the national registers supply free of charge is currently available through it; anything else has to be obtained from the national register.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-05 from the European e-Justice Portal’s own pages, retrieved directly. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The national business registers of the member states. The portal states that company information provided through BRIS is gathered in real time from the business registers of the member states, and that what a user sees is the information filed by the company with the national business register. The EU legislation establishing the interconnection is expressly not aimed at creating a central store of company data. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Commission, which runs the European e-Justice Portal and the BRIS helpdesk. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. The search is served from an embedded Commission application; no external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The “Find a company” service reached from the European e-Justice Portal. Registry type: cross-border-registry-interface, and deliberately nothing else. company-register and business-entity-register were both rejected: this system links national registers and constitutes no record of its own, which is exactly the distinction the type exists to carry. A note on the legal citation: the live portal page cites Directive 2012/17/EU and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/884. The first was codified into Directive (EU) 2017/1132, and the second is no longer in force. The record therefore describes the legal basis in general terms rather than repeating a citation that has been superseded. Coverage extends beyond the EU to Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway, and the record says so rather than implying EU-only coverage. The portal carries its own warning that letters purporting to come from BRIS and demanding payment are fraudulent.

name: VIES VAT number validation
description: VIES is the European Commission service for checking whether a VAT identification number issued by a member state is valid. Each check is run against that member state’s own national VAT database; there is no EU-level VAT database behind it.

operator.name: European Commission, Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union

publicAccess.notes: Open access was observed, not inferred: an anonymous request to the service’s published endpoint returned a complete validation result for a test VAT number on the verification date, with no account, key or credential of any kind. The browser interface itself is a client-rendered application and was not exercised, so no claim is made about a CAPTCHA on that surface.

bestFor: Checking that a counterparty’s EU VAT identification number is valid before treating a cross-border supply as zero-rated.
Confirming, where the issuing member state permits it, that a VAT number belongs to the trader you think it does.
notRecommendedFor: Establishing that a company exists, is incorporated or is solvent. A VAT number is not a company registration and this service does not touch any company register.
Reading an invalid result as proof of wrongdoing. It can mean the number was mistyped, is not activated for cross-border trade, or that the national system was unavailable.
pros: It queries the issuing member state’s own VAT database at the moment of the request, so a positive result reflects national data rather than a cached EU copy.
Access is genuinely open: an anonymous request returned a full result with no account or key, which makes verification reproducible.
Where the member state allows it, the response returns the registered name and address, which turns a number check into an identity check.
cons: Some member states do not permit the name and address to be shown, so a valid number may return no identifying detail at all. That is by design, not a fault.
It confirms only VAT-number validity. It says nothing about incorporation, solvency, tax compliance generally or the trustworthiness of the trader.
An invalid answer has several possible causes and is not by itself evidence that the trader is not registered.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-05 from the Commission’s own service and its published help text, both retrieved directly, and by exercising the service anonymously. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The national VAT databases of the member states. The service’s own help text states that verification is done against the national VAT database corresponding to the selected member state, and that there is no VAT database at Community level. VIES constitutes nothing. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Commission, Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union, which the Commission’s online-services index names as the manager of the site. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. The application is served from the Commission’s own taxation and customs host; no external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The VIES application at ec.europa.eu/taxation_customs/vies/, together with the published validation endpoint the same service exposes. Registry type: tax-verification-system, the only honest fit. corporate-number-database was rejected because the number is a tax identifier rather than a company registration identifier, and because treating a VAT check as a company lookup is precisely the overclaim this record is written to prevent. A URL worth recording: the plausible-looking vies.ec.europa.eu does not resolve at all, and the Commission’s current service index still links the service at its long-standing address. Several legacy help pages under the old .do scheme now return 404 while still being referenced from inside the live application.

name: Tenders Electronic Daily
description: TED is the online supplement to the Official Journal of the European Union for public procurement. Contracting authorities across the EU and the European Economic Area publish their procurement notices there, and the notices are searchable without charge.

operator.name: Publications Office of the European Union

publicAccess.notes: The site states plainly that access to TED is free of charge, and the search result surface was retrieved anonymously with no credential. Registration exists but is for personalised features such as saved searches and alerts, not for reading notices. No CAPTCHA was encountered, but absence was not established and none is asserted.

bestFor: Finding open European public procurement opportunities across all member states in one place.
Reading the official published notice for a European tender, including who is buying and on what terms.
notRecommendedFor: Registering as a supplier. TED publishes notices; it does not hold a supplier register and inclusion in it is not a qualification.
Submitting a bid. Tenders are submitted through the buyer’s own system, not through TED.
recommendedIndustries: Suppliers bidding for European public contracts
pros: It is the official publication venue for European procurement notices, so a notice there is the authoritative published text rather than a re-listing.
Access is free and anonymous, and the site says so in its own words rather than leaving a reader to discover it.
Coverage spans the European Union and the European Economic Area and beyond, with thousands of notices published every working day.
cons: It is a notice database, not a supplier register, a tender-submission system or a funding portal, and it should not be used as any of those.
A published notice records what a buyer announced. It is not a record of who won, unless a separate award notice was also published.
The site cautions that only electronically signed notices published in the Supplement to the Official Journal are authentic.
Publication establishes nothing about a supplier’s eligibility or standing. A notice records that a buyer announced a contract, not that any bidder qualifies for it.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-05 from the site’s own about, legal-notice and search pages, retrieved directly. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The Official Journal of the European Union. TED is the online version of the Supplement to the Official Journal dedicated to European public procurement, and the notice as published there is the official text; the site states that only electronically signed notices published in the Supplement are authentic. The underlying procurement decisions belong to the contracting authorities that publish them. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: Publications Office of the European Union, named on the site as the body that manages it. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. No external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The public search at ted.europa.eu, which the site states is free of charge. Registry type: public-procurement-notice-database, the type added in an earlier wave for exactly this function. procurement-supplier-register was considered and firmly rejected: TED records notices published by buyers, not suppliers admitted to a list, and conflating the two would invert what a reader can conclude from a hit. The record also states what TED is not, because the surrounding EU procurement estate contains separate systems for supplier participation and for funding that are easy to mistake for it.

name: EU Transparency Register
description: The Transparency Register lists interest representatives who seek to influence EU policy and decision-making. It is operated jointly by the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union and the European Commission under a 2021 interinstitutional agreement, and registrants publish a profile of their lobbying and advocacy activity.

operator.name: European Parliament, Council of the European Union and European Commission

publicAccess.notes: The register’s public pages and its search entry point were retrieved anonymously with no credential and no fee. The result application itself is client-rendered and was not exercised, so nothing is asserted about result formatting, export or any CAPTCHA on that surface.

bestFor: Checking whether an organisation lobbying EU institutions is registered, and reading what it declares about its activity and clients.
Understanding which interests are represented on a given EU policy file before relying on a submission or position paper.
notRecommendedFor: Treating registration as accreditation, approval or endorsement by the EU institutions. It is neither, and the register does not vet the truth of a declaration.
Company verification. It records interest representatives and what they declare, not corporate existence or standing.
pros: It is operated jointly by the three main EU institutions rather than by one of them, which is what gives it reach across the institutions.
Registration is backed by conditionality: certain activities in dealings with the institutions are made conditional on being registered, so the incentive to appear is real.
The register can remove an organisation for up to two years where the code of conduct is breached, so entries carry a sanction behind them.
cons: Entries are self-declared. Registration does not verify that what an organisation says about its activities, funding or clients is accurate.
It is not a permission system: being listed is not approval by any EU institution, and absence does not prove an organisation does no advocacy.
The search runs as a client-rendered application that was not exercised, so its behaviour and any export limits were not observed.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-05 from the register’s own governance, legal-references and conditionality pages, retrieved directly. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The register is constituted by the Interinstitutional Agreement of 20 May 2021 between the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union and the European Commission on a mandatory transparency register. The entries themselves are declarations made by the registrants. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: The three signatory institutions jointly. The register states that it is governed by a management board made up of the Secretaries-General of the Parliament, the Council and the Commission, supported by a joint secretariat staffed from all three. The operator field names the three institutions rather than any one of them, because naming a single institution would misstate who is answerable. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. No external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The public register search at transparency-register.europa.eu. Participation model, determined rather than flattened: the register describes registration as having become de facto mandatory in 2021, delivered through conditionality — certain activities in dealings with the institutions are made conditional on registration, and the register notes for example that only registered stakeholders can access some institutional settings. It is therefore neither purely voluntary nor a legal duty on all organisations, and the record says so in those terms. Registry type: public-filing-database, because the content is declarations filed by registrants. professional-licence-register and regulated-operator-register were both rejected: registration is not an authorisation to operate and confers no permission.

name: ESMA list of registered and certified credit rating agencies
description: ESMA publishes the list of credit rating agencies registered or certified under the Credit Rating Agencies Regulation. ESMA is the direct supervisor of credit rating agencies in the European Union, so the registration decisions behind this list are its own rather than compiled from national authorities.
officialName: List of registered or certified credit rating agencies

publicAccess.notes: The list is published as a table on the page itself and was retrieved anonymously with no credential and no fee, showing each agency’s name, country of residence, status, effective date and legal entity identifier. No search URL is published because the page presents the whole list rather than a query interface.

bestFor: Confirming that a credit rating agency is registered or certified to issue ratings usable for regulatory purposes in the EU.
Reading an agency’s registration status, effective date and legal entity identifier from the supervisor’s own published list.
notRecommendedFor: Assessing the quality of an agency’s ratings. The list records regulatory status, not analytical performance.
General company verification, which is a matter for national business registers.
recommendedIndustries: Credit rating agencies operating in the European Union
pros: ESMA supervises credit rating agencies directly, so this list reflects its own registration decisions rather than a compilation of national ones.
The list is published under a statutory duty and states that it is updated within five working days of a registration or certification decision.
Each entry carries a legal entity identifier, which makes an agency identifiable across other financial datasets without name matching.
cons: It covers credit rating agencies only. It is not a general register of financial firms, and other ESMA registers rest on entirely different legal bases.
The page notes that the Commission republishes the list in the Official Journal within thirty days, so the two can differ for a period.
Registration records that an agency meets regulatory requirements. It is not an opinion on its ratings or its conduct.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-05 from ESMA’s own published list, retrieved directly. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: ESMA itself. The page states that the agencies listed have been registered or certified in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1060/2009, and that the list is published by ESMA under Article 18(3) of that regulation. This is deliberately unlike most other EU financial registers, which compile decisions taken by national competent authorities: for credit rating agencies ESMA is the single direct supervisor, so it is the source of record. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Securities and Markets Authority. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. The list is served as part of ESMA’s own site; no external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The published list on ESMA’s credit rating agencies pages. Scope discipline: ESMA operates a large number of separate registers and databases resting on different regulations, and its common registers portal is a search layer over them rather than one register. That portal was assessed and deliberately not published, because publishing it would merge unrelated databases into a single record. This record covers one register with one legal basis, which is the only honest unit here.

name: EBA credit institutions register
description: The European Banking Authority publishes a register of credit institutions authorised in the European Economic Area. The authorisations themselves are granted by national authorities; the EBA assembles their notifications into one European view.

publicAccess.notes: The describing page was retrieved anonymously, but the register application itself sits behind a separate interface that was not exercised, so no search behaviour is asserted and no search URL is published.

bestFor: Checking whether a bank is authorised as a credit institution somewhere in the European Economic Area, and by which national authority.
Getting a single European view of authorised credit institutions rather than querying each national regulator in turn.
notRecommendedFor: Treating the EBA as the authorising body. Licensing credit institutions remains with the national authorities, and the EBA states this.
Relying on it as legally definitive. The EBA compiles it from national notifications and does not warrant the underlying data.
recommendedIndustries: Credit institutions authorised in the European Economic Area
pros: It gathers authorisation data from every national authority in the European Economic Area into one place, which no single national register does.
The EBA states plainly that it built the register solely from information supplied by national authorities, so the provenance of every entry is explicit.
It makes the split between European assembly and national authorisation legible rather than leaving a reader to assume the EBA licenses banks.
cons: The EBA does not grant the licences. It states that granting licences to credit institutions remains with the national authorities.
It is a compilation. An entry reflects what a national authority notified, and the EBA does not guarantee that the underlying information is accurate or current.
The register application was not exercised, so its search behaviour, coverage of historical entries and export options were not observed.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-05 from the EBA’s own register pages, retrieved directly. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The national competent authorities of the European Economic Area, which grant the authorisations. The EBA states that the register was set up solely on the basis of information supplied by those authorities, and that the granting of licences to credit institutions remains under their remit. The EBA is not the source of record. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Banking Authority, which compiles and publishes the register. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. The register application is served from a separate EBA interface; no external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The register pages on the EBA site and the register application reached from them. Shared host: this record and the EBA payment and electronic money institutions register are two legally distinct registers published on one official host, so both declare resourceIdentity rather than being merged. They rest on different legislation and cover different populations; collapsing them would be the same error as merging unrelated supervisory databases into one broad record.

name: EBA register of payment and electronic money institutions
description: The European Banking Authority publishes a central register of payment institutions and electronic money institutions authorised or registered under the second Payment Services Directive. The authorisations are granted by national authorities, which supply the information the register contains.
officialName: Register of payment and electronic money institutions under PSD2

publicAccess.notes: The EBA documents that public users can search the central register free of charge, which is why free search is recorded. The register application itself was not exercised, so no search URL is published and no claim is made about login, CAPTCHA or export.

bestFor: Checking whether a payment or e-money firm is authorised or registered under the second Payment Services Directive, and in which member state.
Verifying a fintech counterparty’s regulatory status across Europe from one register rather than many national ones.
notRecommendedFor: Treating the EBA as the authorising body. Authorisation is granted by the national authority, and the EBA compiles what it is told.
Assuming an entry proves a firm is safe or well run. It records an authorisation, not conduct or solvency.
recommendedIndustries: Payment institutions and electronic money institutions in the European Economic Area
pros: The EBA documents that public users can search the central register free of charge, so the access position is stated by the operator rather than assumed.
It gives one European view of payment and e-money authorisations, which matters because these firms passport across borders.
The provenance is explicit: the EBA states that national competent authorities provide the information the register contains.
cons: It is a compilation, not the authorisation itself. Under the directive, granting authorisation to payment institutions rests with the national authorities.
The EBA states that it built the register solely from information supplied by national authorities and does not warrant that information.
The register application was not exercised, so its search behaviour and export options were not observed and no search URL is published.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-05 from the EBA’s own register pages, retrieved directly. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The national competent authorities, which authorise and register payment and electronic money institutions. The EBA states that national competent authorities provide the information contained in the register, and that under Article 11 of the second Payment Services Directive the granting of authorisation to payment institutions is theirs. The EBA is not the source of record. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Banking Authority, which keeps and publishes the central register under the directive. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. The register application is served from a separate EBA interface; no external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The register pages on the EBA site and the register application reached from them. The EBA documents that public users can search it free of charge. Shared host: this record and the EBA credit institutions register are two legally distinct registers on one official host and both declare resourceIdentity. Access level is partially-open rather than open: free public search is documented by the operator, but the application was not exercised, so the remaining access facts stay null instead of being completed by assumption.

name: EIOPA register of insurance undertakings
description: The European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority publishes a register of insurance undertakings authorised in the European Economic Area. It represents information supplied by the national supervisory authorities and is updated weekly.

operator.name: European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority

publicAccess.notes: The register page was retrieved anonymously, but it states that JavaScript is required and the register content is client-rendered, so no search behaviour was observed, no search URL is published and every access boolean stays null.

bestFor: Checking whether an insurer is authorised in the European Economic Area and which national supervisor authorised it.
Getting a European view of authorised insurance undertakings without querying each national supervisor separately.
notRecommendedFor: Treating EIOPA as the authorising supervisor. Authorisation is national, and this register represents information supplied by national authorities.
Checking insurance intermediaries, which are a different population and are not in this register.
recommendedIndustries: Insurance undertakings authorised in the European Economic Area
pros: It assembles authorisation data from the national supervisors of the whole European Economic Area into a single register.
EIOPA states that the register is updated weekly, so the refresh cadence is published rather than left unstated.
It is clearly scoped to undertakings, which keeps it distinct from the separate and much weaker position on intermediaries.
cons: It is a representation of information supplied by national authorities, not an authorisation decision by EIOPA.
The register page requires JavaScript and its content is client-rendered, so its search behaviour and export options were not observed.
An entry records authorisation. It is not a statement about an insurer’s solvency, conduct or claims handling.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-05 from EIOPA’s own register pages, retrieved directly. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The national supervisory authorities of the European Economic Area, which authorise insurance undertakings. EIOPA states that the register is a representation of the information supplied to it, so the constitutive decisions sit nationally. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, which compiles and publishes the register. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. No external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The register at register.eiopa.europa.eu, which is a separate host from EIOPA’s main site and carries the registers rather than the institutional content. Scope discipline: EIOPA’s separate page on insurance intermediaries was assessed and deliberately not published. It is a country-by-country table of links to national registers containing no intermediary records of its own, which is a menu rather than a register, and publishing it would imply an EU-wide intermediary register that does not currently exist.

name: EDES exclusion database
description: The European Commission publishes the list of persons and entities excluded from participating in EU-funded award procedures, or subject to a financial penalty, under the Early Detection and Exclusion System. Publication is provided for by the Financial Regulation and is reserved for the most severe cases.
officialName: Early Detection and Exclusion System (EDES) database

publicAccess.notes: The published list appears on the Commission page itself and was retrieved anonymously with no credential and no fee. It is a published list rather than a query interface, so no search URL is published. Only cases where publication was decided appear; the wider exclusion system is not public.

bestFor: Checking whether a person or entity has been publicly excluded from EU-funded award procedures, and for what period.
Due diligence on a prospective partner in an EU-funded project, alongside national debarment sources.
notRecommendedFor: Concluding that an absent party has never been excluded. Only cases where publication was specifically decided appear here.
Any inference about sanctions or restrictions outside EU-funded procedures, which this list does not cover.
recommendedIndustries: Contractors and beneficiaries of EU-funded procedures
pros: It is the Commission’s own published exclusion list, so an entry is the authoritative record of the measure rather than a report of it.
Each entry states the period of the exclusion, so a reader can tell whether a measure is current.
It is openly readable with no account, which is unusual for exclusion data and makes it genuinely checkable.
cons: It is deliberately partial. The Commission states that the list concerns only the cases for which a decision to publish was taken, so absence proves nothing.
Entries are removed as soon as the exclusion ends, and a financial penalty is removed six months after payment, so the list is not a historical archive.
It covers exclusion from EU-funded procedures only, and says nothing about restrictions imposed under any other regime.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-05 from the Commission’s own EDES pages, retrieved directly. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The European Commission, acting under the Financial Regulation. The page states that publication of an EDES measure is done in accordance with the relevant legal framework and points to Article 142 of the Financial Regulation. The exclusion decision is the Commission’s own, so unlike most records in this wave the EU institution is the source of record. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Commission. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. The list is published as part of the Commission’s own site; no external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The published list on the Commission’s EDES pages. Registry type: exclusion-and-debarment-register, which the vocabulary defines for exactly this function and which the dataset already uses for national equivalents. The record is explicit that the published list is a subset: the Commission states that it covers only cases for which a decision to publish was taken, and that entries are removed when the exclusion ends. A reader who treated absence from this list as proof that a party has never been excluded, or as proof of unrestricted standing anywhere else, would be wrong, and the record says so rather than leaving it implied.

name: EUIPO eSearch plus
description: eSearch plus is the European Union Intellectual Property Office’s public search application over its own registers of EU trade marks and EU designs. Results are presented under separate tabs for trade marks, designs, owners and representatives.

publicAccess.notes: The application shell was retrieved anonymously and identifies itself, but no search was executed and no result list was seen, so no search behaviour is asserted and no search URL is published. The office’s main site refuses some automated requests while serving a normal browser, so a refusal there is not evidence that a page is gone.

bestFor: Checking the status, owner and history of an EU trade mark or an EU design in the office’s own records.
Establishing whether a mark or design is already protected at EU level before filing.
notRecommendedFor: Searching national rights held by member state offices, which are reached through the separate aggregation portals rather than here.
Company verification. This covers industrial property rights, not the existence of a business.
recommendedIndustries: Holders and applicants of EU trade marks and EU designs
pros: It is the office’s own application over its own registers, so it is the authoritative public view of an EU trade mark or EU design rather than a copy.
Trade marks, designs, owners and representatives are presented under separate tabs, so distinct populations are not blended into one undifferentiated result.
One office keeps both registers, so a single search covers two rights that elsewhere require two systems.
cons: It is the search interface over the registers, not the registers themselves. The register is the instrument the office is obliged by regulation to keep.
It covers EU-level rights only. National marks and designs are not in it, and their absence here proves nothing about them.
No search was executed during verification, so the fee position, any rate limit and any CAPTCHA are unestablished and are not asserted.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-06 from the application itself and from the office’s own search hub, retrieved directly. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The Registers kept by EUIPO under the EU trade mark and EU design regulations. The regulations separate the instrument from the software: the office is obliged to keep a Register, and separately to store the particulars in an electronic database. The Register is the source of record; this application is the view over the database. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Union Intellectual Property Office, an agency of the European Union. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. The application is served from the office’s own host; no external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The eSearch plus application, listed on the office’s own search hub alongside its case-law, aggregation and classification tools. Registry types: trademark-register and registered-design-register are recorded separately, as the vocabulary requires even where one office keeps both. professional-licence-register was considered for the representatives tab and rejected: the office maintains a list of professional representatives, but it issues no licence, and a search tab is not a separate register. Scoping decision: there is no separate EUIPO trade mark search and EUIPO design search — they are one application with tabs, so this is one record rather than two, and certainly not one record per tab. A naming note: the right formerly called a registered Community design is now the registered EU design, and the register formerly called the Register of Community designs is now the Register of EU designs. The older wording is obsolete and is deliberately not used here.

name: TMview
description: TMview is the search portal of the European Union Intellectual Property Network that searches trade mark applications and registrations held by participating offices — national offices in the EU, the EUIPO, and offices outside the EU. It aggregates data supplied by those offices and is not itself a trade mark register.

publicAccess.notes: The portal serves a JavaScript application shell that carries no identifying text of its own, so identity and function rest on the office’s own current search hub, which lists TMview and describes what it covers. No search was executed, so every access boolean stays null and no search URL is published. A response on this host is not by itself evidence that a particular resource exists, because unmatched paths also return a shell.

bestFor: Searching trade marks across many national offices and the EU office at once, which no single register offers.
Establishing whether a similar mark already exists somewhere in Europe before choosing where to file.
notRecommendedFor: Treating a result as the register entry. The records belong to the office that issued them, and that office is where the authoritative entry lives.
Concluding a mark is free because it is absent. Coverage depends on which offices participate and on how current each office’s supply is.
recommendedIndustries: Trade mark applicants and holders searching across European and international offices
pros: One search reaches trade mark data from participating offices at national, EU and international level, which is what it exists to do.
It is operated within the official European Union Intellectual Property Network rather than by a commercial aggregator.
It keeps the aggregation role explicit, so a user can go back to the issuing office for the authoritative record.
cons: It is an aggregation portal, not a register. It does not constitute any right and establishes nothing on its own.
Coverage is defined by which offices participate and by what each supplies, so it is not a complete picture of trade marks in Europe.
The portal is a client-rendered application that could not be exercised, so its search behaviour, filters and export options were not observed.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-06 from the office’s own search hub, retrieved directly, because the portal itself serves an identity-free application shell. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The participating offices that issue the rights. The office’s own hub describes TMview as covering trade marks of all participating official trade mark offices at national, international and EU level, which places the records with those offices. TMview constitutes nothing. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Union Intellectual Property Office, which operates the portal within the European Union Intellectual Property Network. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: The shared network application at tmdn.org, which serves both this portal and the design portal from one codebase. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The TMview portal on the network host. Registry type: cross-border-registry-interface, and deliberately nothing else. trademark-register was proposed and rejected as a direct contradiction: a record cannot state three times that a system is not a register and then carry the register type. Shared host: this record and DesignView sit on one official host and both declare resourceIdentity. They are kept as two records because they cover two different rights with two different participating-office populations and are described separately by the office, not because their URLs differ.

name: DesignView
description: DesignView is the design search portal of the European Union Intellectual Property Network. The office describes it as providing access to its own database of registered designs together with the databases of other national registries, so it aggregates data from participating offices rather than constituting a register.

publicAccess.notes: The portal serves a JavaScript application shell with no identifying text of its own, so identity and function rest on the office’s own description of the service. No search was executed, so every access boolean stays null and no search URL is published.

bestFor: Searching designs across the EU office and participating national registries in one place.
Checking whether a similar design is already on a European register before filing.
notRecommendedFor: Treating a result as the register entry. The authoritative record sits with the office that registered the design.
Concluding a design is free because it is absent, since coverage depends on which registries participate.
recommendedIndustries: Design applicants and holders searching across European offices
pros: It reaches the EU office’s design database and other national registries together, which no single national registry does.
It is operated within the official European Union Intellectual Property Network rather than by a commercial aggregator.
It is scoped to designs, which keeps it from being confused with the trade mark portal that shares its platform.
cons: It is an aggregation portal, not a register. It constitutes no design right and establishes nothing on its own.
Coverage depends on which registries participate and on what each supplies, so absence is not evidence that a design is unprotected.
The portal is a client-rendered application that could not be exercised, so its search behaviour and export options were not observed.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-06 from the office’s own description of the service, retrieved directly, because the portal itself serves an identity-free application shell. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The offices that register the designs. The office describes DesignView as providing access to its own database of registered designs along with the databases of other national registries, which places the records with those offices rather than with the portal. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Union Intellectual Property Office, which operates the portal within the European Union Intellectual Property Network. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: The shared network application at tmdn.org, which serves both this portal and the trade mark portal from one codebase. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The DesignView portal on the network host. Registry type: cross-border-registry-interface only. registered-design-register was rejected for the same reason the trade mark type was rejected on the sibling portal: a record must not deny being a register and then carry the register type. Shared host: this record and TMview both declare resourceIdentity. A naming note carried from this wave’s research: the EU right is now the registered EU design and the register is the Register of EU designs, the earlier Community wording having been replaced.

name: EUDAMED
description: EUDAMED is the European database on medical devices established by the medical devices and in vitro diagnostic regulations. It holds registrations of economic operators, devices and certificates, and its first four modules became mandatory on 28 May 2026.

operator.name: European Commission, Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety

publicAccess.notes: The public site serves a JavaScript application shell, so identity, function and current status rest on the Commission’s own medical devices pages. No search was executed, so every access boolean stays null and no search URL is published.

bestFor: Checking whether a medical device economic operator is registered in the EU database and under which role.
Following the phased introduction of EU medical device registration obligations from the responsible authority’s own system.
notRecommendedFor: Treating a registration as a safety approval. Registration records that an operator or device has been entered, not that the device has been assessed as safe.
Assuming complete coverage. The modules became mandatory only recently and earlier use was voluntary, so historical completeness is limited.
recommendedIndustries: Medical device manufacturers, importers and authorised representatives in the EU
pros: It is established directly by the medical devices and in vitro diagnostic regulations rather than by administrative practice.
Its first four modules became mandatory on 28 May 2026, so the data has moved from voluntary submission to a legal obligation.
It brings economic operator, device and certificate registration into one European system rather than leaving it to national registers.
cons: The public site is a client-rendered application that could not be exercised, so its search behaviour and coverage of each module were not observed.
It does not certify devices. Conformity assessment is carried out by notified bodies, and an entry is not a statement that a device is safe or effective.
Because mandatory use began recently, absence of an operator or device is not evidence that it does not exist or is not lawfully placed on the market.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-06 from the Commission’s own medical devices pages, retrieved directly, because the public application serves an identity-free shell. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The database is established by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices. Registrations are made by economic operators and certificates are issued by notified bodies, so the underlying acts are theirs; the database records them. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Commission, through the directorate responsible for health and food safety. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. No external supplier is named on any page fetched, and none is asserted. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The public EUDAMED site on the Commission’s tools host. Status, established rather than assumed: the Commission announced that the first four modules of EUDAMED became mandatory on 28 May 2026. A characterisation of EUDAMED as still voluntary, which was accurate for years, is now out of date, and this record deliberately states the current position. Registry type: regulated-operator-register, because the indexed population that a reader can act on is registered economic operators in a regulated sector. The record does not claim the public interface is complete across all modules, because that was not observed.

name: ECHA CHEM
description: ECHA CHEM is the European Chemicals Agency’s platform for information on substances placed on the EU market. It publishes information from REACH registration dossiers filed with the agency, together with classification and labelling entries and cross-references to other EU regulatory regimes.

publicAccess.notes: Free credential-free access was observed against the platform’s public substance interface, which returned complete substance records without any account. The rendered interface itself is a client-side application and was not exercised, so no claim is made about its on-screen filters, exports or any CAPTCHA. The agency’s main site refused automated requests behind a web application firewall, which is a bot filter rather than an outage.

bestFor: Checking whether a substance has been registered under the EU chemicals regulation and reading the information published from its dossier.
Finding a substance’s harmonised or notified classification and the EU regulatory regimes it falls under.
notRecommendedFor: Treating registration as approval. The agency does not thereby declare a substance safe, and it checks only a proportion of dossiers.
Reading absence as illegality, since low-volume substances, polymers and other exempt categories are not registrable at all.
recommendedIndustries: Manufacturers and importers of chemical substances in the EU
pros: The dossiers are filed with the agency itself, so for the registration this is genuinely the source of record rather than a publication layer over someone else’s register.
Free access without any account was observed directly against the public substance interface, which makes checks reproducible.
One substance record carries the registration status alongside classification entries and cross-references to other EU regimes, so related obligations are visible together.
cons: Registration is a filing duty, not a permission. The registrant asserts the data and bears responsibility for it, and the agency does not thereby verify the dossier.
The platform reflects rather than constitutes the other lists shown on a substance page, such as harmonised classification, which originates in EU legal acts adopted elsewhere.
Migration from the agency’s older chemical search pages is still in progress, so for some purposes both surfaces may still need consulting.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-06 against the platform’s own public substance interface, which returned live records anonymously. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: Mixed, and deliberately stated as such. For the REACH registration the agency IS the source of record: the dossier is filed with it and it is obliged to publish specified information from that dossier. For the other lists surfaced on a substance page — harmonised classification, inventory entries and downstream sectoral regimes — the source is the underlying EU legal act adopted elsewhere, which the platform reflects rather than constitutes. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Chemicals Agency. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: The agency’s own substance and dossier services, served as a client-side application on the platform host. No external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The ECHA CHEM platform and its public substance interface. Registry type: public-filing-database, because a registration is a dossier filed by an identifiable legal entity with a regulator and published by law, which is what the type describes. The record deliberately avoids claiming that the platform has fully replaced the agency’s older chemical search pages: migration is stated by the agency to be continuing, and an unqualified supersession claim did not survive checking. Access is recorded as partially-open rather than open because free credential-free retrieval was observed on the public data interface while the rendered application was never exercised.

name: European Investment Bank exclusion decisions
description: The European Investment Bank publishes the entities currently subject to an exclusion decision or a settlement agreement under its exclusion policy. Each entry names the entity, its country of incorporation, the nature and validity period of the decision, and the type of proceedings.
officialName: Entities subject to an exclusion decision or a settlement agreement

publicAccess.notes: The list is published as a table on the page itself and was retrieved anonymously with no credential and no fee. There is no search interface over it, so free search is left unstated rather than claimed: a reader reads the published list rather than querying it.

bestFor: Checking whether an entity is currently excluded from bank-financed activity, and until when.
Due diligence on a prospective partner in a project financed by the bank, alongside the Commission’s own exclusion list.
notRecommendedFor: Concluding that an absent entity has never been excluded. Only entities currently publicly subject to a decision appear.
Any inference beyond bank-financed activity. This is not a general debarment list and says nothing about other regimes.
recommendedIndustries: Counterparties and contractors in projects financed by the European Investment Bank
pros: Each entry states the nature of the decision and its validity dates, so a reader can tell what was imposed and whether it is still running.
It is published openly with no account and no fee, which is unusual for exclusion data.
It distinguishes exclusion decisions from settlement agreements and conditional outcomes rather than flattening them into one status.
cons: It is a published list rather than a searchable register, so there is no query interface and no export.
It shows only entities currently publicly subject to a decision, so absence proves nothing about past conduct or past exclusions.
It is confined to the bank’s own exclusion regime and does not cover exclusion from other EU programmes.
editorNotes: Verified 2026-08-06 from the bank’s own exclusion page, retrieved directly, with the published table of entities read in full. FOUR ROLES, determined separately. LEGAL SOURCE OF RECORD: The European Investment Bank, acting under its own exclusion policy. Exclusion decisions and settlement agreements are the bank’s own acts, so unlike most records in the EU set the institution here is the source of record. RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITY: European Investment Bank. TECHNICAL PLATFORM: Not separately established. The list is published as part of the bank’s own site; no external supplier is named on any page fetched. PUBLIC ACCESS INTERFACE: The published table on the bank’s exclusion page. Registry type: exclusion-and-debarment-register, the same type as the Commission’s own exclusion database, which this record is related to but does not duplicate: the two rest on different instruments, cover different populations and are published by different institutions. Access: free search is deliberately left unstated rather than recorded as true, because there is no search surface at all — the page publishes a table. An earlier draft asserted free search and that did not survive checking.
